content: Chronic hepatitis B infection is defined as the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the blood for a minimum of six months. However, interpreting hepatitis B virus (HBV) serological tests can be complex. The most commonly used serological markers for HBV testing include HBsAg, total anti-HBc (hepatitis B core antibody), and anti-HBs (antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen). Testing often involves a combination of HBsAg detection followed by either hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) testing or nucleic acid testing (NAT). HBsAg detection can be performed using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or immunoassays. RDTs designed for screening include various formats such as solid-phase assays, flow-through assays, agglutination tests, and lateral-flow assays, with the majority being immunochromatographic assays. Immunoassays, on the other hand, utilize either polyclonal or monoclonal anti-HBs antibodies to detect HBsAg. Advances in HBV detection technologies have created new opportunities to improve screening, referral, and treatment processes. Existing systematic reviews on hepatitis B testing have primarily focused on point-of-care (POC) tests, including those with unclear reference standards or those not suitable for assessing diagnostic accuracy in real-world settings. The objective of this review was to identify quantitative evidence on the sensitivity and specificity of assays used to detect hepatitis B antibodies, synthesize the findings, and inform diagnostic models. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare the clinical performance of both RDTs and laboratory-based immunoassays while addressing diagnostic accuracy in the context of HIV co-infection. The review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of available assays for detecting HBsAg among individuals identified for hepatitis B testing. The reference standard for comparison was a laboratory-based enzyme immunoassay (EIA), which may include one or more HBsAg enzyme immunoassays, with or without neutralization for confirmation. As a secondary analysis, the review also assessed the accuracy of HBsAg assays compared to a nucleic acid amplification test (NAT) reference standard. A comprehensive literature search was conducted by a medical librarian with expertise in systematic reviews. Databases searched included MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Science Citation Index Expanded, SCOPUS, and others. The search was supplemented by contacting researchers and experts in the field and reviewing references from relevant articles. The review was registered in PROSPERO and followed PRISMA guidelines. Study selection involved three stages: initial screening of titles and abstracts, full-text review of selected articles, and resolution of discrepancies through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Inclusion criteria encompassed case-control, cross-sectional, cohort studies, and randomized trials evaluating HBsAg tests published up to May 2015. Excluded studies included conference abstracts, reviews, studies not focused on sensitivity and specificity, and those unrelated to diagnostic purposes. Eligible studies included original data from patient specimens across all age groups, settings, and countries, using various specimen types such as whole blood, plasma, or serum. Studies using commercial HBsAg tests were included, while in-house tests or outdated laboratory-based immunoassays were excluded. The reference standard for HBsAg detection was a commercially available immunoassay, with NAT-based reference standards included for supplementary analysis. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers and included variables such as study design, sample size, specimen type, and raw diagnostic data (e.g., true positives, false negatives). The quality of studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, which evaluates bias and applicability concerns in domains such as patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow/timing. The GRADE system was used to rate the strength of evidence based on factors such as consistency, precision, and reporting bias. Meta-analysis was conducted using standard methods for diagnostic accuracy, calculating pooled sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed, and meta-regression was performed to explore sources of variability. The review identified 33 studies for primary analysis, comparing RDTs and laboratory-based immunoassays against an immunoassay reference standard. These studies originated from 23 countries and included a range of populations, such as healthy volunteers, at-risk groups (e.g., pregnant women, incarcerated individuals), and patients with confirmed hepatitis B. Most studies were conducted in laboratory settings, with some performed in the field. Specimen types included serum, plasma, and whole blood. The pooled diagnostic accuracy of RDTs compared to EIAs showed significant heterogeneity across studies. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on factors such as study year, geographical region, specimen type, and patient HIV status. The review also evaluated the performance of specific RDT brands, with Determine HBsAg being the most frequently studied. In conclusion, this systematic review provides a comprehensive evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of HBsAg assays, highlighting the variability in performance across different test types, settings, and populations. The findings underscore the importance of selecting appropriate diagnostic tools for hepatitis B screening, particularly in resource-limited settings and among populations with co-existing conditions such as HIV.
